module_title: The Core Causes of Inflation (Demand vs. Cost)
introduction: Why do prices rise? In macroeconomics, there are two primary theoretical reasons: Either the market has suddenly generated too much 'Demand', or the 'Cost' of manufacturing the goods has suddenly spiked.

core_concepts.title: 1. Demand-Pull Inflation
core_concepts.description: Occurs when Aggregate Demand in the economy exceeds Aggregate Supply. In simple terms: 'Too much money chasing too few goods'. Causes: A sudden increase in population, the government printing too much money, or the RBI lowering interest rates (giving people cheap loans to spend).

core_concepts.title: 2. Cost-Push Inflation
core_concepts.description: Occurs when the 'Cost of Production' for companies goes up. If raw materials (like crude oil), transportation, or labor wages become expensive, companies will 'push' this extra cost onto the consumer by raising the final price of the product. This is also called a 'Supply Shock'.

core_concepts.title: 3. Built-in (Structural) Inflation
core_concepts.description: This is driven by the 'Wage-Price Spiral'. When workers see that inflation is rising, they demand higher salaries to survive. When companies pay higher salaries (increased costs), they raise the prices of their goods to maintain profits, prompting workers to demand even higher salaries. It becomes an endless loop.

important_entities.name: Supply Shock
important_entities.significance: In India, the biggest trigger for Cost-Push inflation is international 'Crude Oil' prices. When oil becomes expensive, transportation becomes expensive, which instantly makes everything from vegetables to electronics more expensive.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Question: 'If the RBI injects massive amounts of cash into the economy, which type of inflation occurs?' Answer: 'Demand-Pull'. By giving people more money, you are artificially boosting their 'demand' for goods.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Demand 'Pulls' prices up from the consumer side (buyers want more). Cost 'Pushes' prices up from the producer side (factories are struggling).

exam_strategy_tips: The phrase 'Too much money chasing too few goods' was coined by economist Milton Friedman and is the universal definition of Demand-Pull inflation. UPSC frequently uses this exact quote.
